title.en: Batara Guru Descends to Luwu: The Opening of the La Galigo
title.zh: 巴塔拉·古魯降臨盧武：《加利戈》開篇

region.en: Luwu, South Sulawesi (middle world of the Bugis)
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西盧武（布吉人之中界）

texts.period: La Galigo (Sureq Galigo) epic tradition, dating from approximately the 14th century, rooted in oral tradition

source.archive: UNESCO Memory of the World Register (La Galigo, Indonesia and the Netherlands)
source.work: La Galigo epic (Bugis language, c. 14th century origins); MSS in the Museum La Galigo, Makassar, and the University Library of Leiden

summary.en: The Bugis myth par excellence: in the La Galigo, the most voluminous literary work known (an estimated 6,000 folio pages), the god Batara Guru descends from the upper world to the middle world in the land of Luwu, South Sulawesi, and his children and grandchildren people it — above all the hero Sawerigading and his son La Galigo, whose name the whole epic carries.
summary.zh: 布吉人至高之神話：在《加利戈》（Sureq Galigo，已知最浩繁之文學作品，約六千葉）中，神明巴塔拉·古魯自上界降臨南蘇拉威西盧武之地（中界），其子孫繁衍其間——尤以英雄薩維里加丁及其子加利戈為最，整部史詩即以其子命名。

sensitivity.note: Living Bugis identity-epic (Memory of the World, 2011); the epic is still performed (I La Galigo, 2004); paraphrase only, respect the community's ownership.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the standard La Galigo narrative as summarized in the UNESCO nomination and published bilingual editions (Bugis-Indonesian, 1995 and 2000); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The La Galigo is the myth of the Bugis people par excellence — a poetic text in strict metre, composed in a difficult Bugis literary idiom, of pre-Islamic epic-mythological content, running to an estimated six thousand folio pages across manuscripts scattered from Makassar to Leiden, London and Washington. Its story opens in heaven and descends to Sulawesi.

BEGINNING: THE THREE WORLDS. The Bugis cosmos of the epic is arranged in levels: the upper world of the gods, the middle world of men, and the underworld. The upper world is troubled; its people seek a remedy in marriage and descent, and the god Batara Guru is sent down — or comes down of his own heroic motion — to the middle world, to the land of Luwu in the south of Sulawesi.

MIDDLE: THE DIVINE DESCENT IN LUWU. Batara Guru takes his place among the rulers of the middle world, and his marriage and his line fuse heaven with the Bugis country: his descendants are the heroic generations of the epic, endowed with the beauty, strength and appetites of gods living at human scale. The epic follows them through courtship, feud, voyage and ceremony — a chronicle of a world in which the divine continues to walk.

END: SAWERIGADING AND LA GALIGO. The greatest of the line is Sawerigading, the central hero, whose voyages andwhose doom the epic follows; his son La Galigo, born of the later generations, gives the work its name — 'Sureq Galigo', the song of Galigo. The two nominated manuscripts make this concrete: one holds the complete episode of the journey of Sawerigading and his son La Galigo to Senrijawa; the other, in twelve volumes by the Bugis queen Colliq Pujié of Pancana, preserves the longest known fragment. The epic thus ends where it is named: with the family of the descended god becoming the ancestry and identity of the Bugis people.

FUNCTIONS. The opening cycle (1) grounds Bugis kingship in divine descent landed at Luwu; (2) organizes the epic's moral world around marriages that join or sunder the levels; (3) makes Sulawesi's landscape the stage of divine biography; and (4) provides, in Sawerigading's line, the charter-hero of the southern Sulawesi courts. The epic's scale frames the descent: at an estimated six thousand folio pages the La Galigo exceeds every other epic on record, and no single manuscript contains the whole; the Makassar museum's 217-page manuscript holds the Senrijawa journey complete, and the Leiden twelve-volume copy — written by the Bugis queen Colliq Pujie of Pancana with the scholar B. F. Matthes — preserves the longest known fragment. The descent of Batara Guru is thus the doorway to a whole epic world of courts, voyages, weddings and wars in which divine qualities continue at human scale. The epic's standing in South Sulawesi is civic as much as literary: roads, museums and a university carry the names of La Galigo's heroes, and Robert Wilson's theatre adaptation I La Galigo carried the poetry to world stages in 2004 — a living myth whose afterlife is still being written.
narrative.zh: 《加利戈》乃布吉民族之至高神話——格律嚴謹、以佶屈之布吉文學語言寫成、前伊斯蘭時期之神話史詩，散於望加錫、萊頓、倫敦、華盛頓諸館之手稿合計約六千葉。其故事自天堂開篇而降至蘇拉威西。開篇：布吉宇宙分層——上界諸神、中界人間、下界冥府；上界有事，乃遣神明巴塔拉·古魯下降中界——南蘇拉威西盧武之地。中段：巴塔拉·古魯居中界諸王之間，其婚姻與後裔將天堂與布吉大地熔為一體：史詩追述諸英雄世代之求偶、仇殺、航行與儀典——神性仍行走人間之編年史。結尾：世系之最偉者薩維里加丁——史詩之中樞英雄——其航行與命運貫穿全篇；其子加利戈使全作得名『加利戈之歌』。兩部提名手稿為證：一部載薩維里加丁父子赴三里爪哇之完整篇章；另一部為潘恰納女君科利·普吉所書十二巨冊，存已知最長殘篇。史詩終於其得名處：降神之家成為布吉民族之祖源與認同。功能：以盧武降神立布吉王權之神裔、以聯姻組織史詩之道德世界、以蘇拉威西山水為神明傳記之舞臺、並為南蘇拉威西宮廷提供憲章英雄。

title.en: Sawerigading and the Forbidden Twin: The Ship That Could Not Touch Home
title.zh: 薩維里加丁與禁忌的孿生：不能靠岸的船

region.en: Luwu and the open sea, South Sulawesi
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西盧武與外海

texts.period: La Galigo epic tradition (Bugis); c. 14th century origins

source.archive: UNESCO Memory of the World Register (La Galigo)

summary.en: The central knot of the Sawerigading cycle: the hero's desire for his own twin sister is forbidden, and his punishment is the sea. He builds a great ship and sails away; the ship is fated never to touch the shore it longs for, and the hero's exile becomes the great Bugis image of the sea as the price of a broken boundary.
summary.zh: 薩維里加丁故事之樞紐：英雄欲娶自己孿生妹妹，此乃禁忌；其罰即是海洋。他造巨舟遠航；此船命定不能靠近思慕之岸——英雄之放逐，成為布吉人『破界之價是海』之偉大意象。

sensitivity.note: La Galigo core episode; incest-twin taboo treated as literary material.

passages.text: Sawerigading, the hero of the line of Batara Guru, desires the twin born with him — and the desire is impossible: the twin taboo stands across it as the boundary the Bugis world will not move. He builds a great ship and puts out to sea; the ship is fated never to come to rest at the shore of his desire, and his voyaging becomes the epic's image of exile — the sea as the price of the broken boundary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the La Galigo Sawerigading cycle; not verbatim.

title.en: Sawerigading Goes Down: The Hero Becomes King of the Underworld
title.zh: 薩維里加丁下行：英雄成為冥府之王

region.en: Wewangriu and the underworld (Peretui), Bugis cosmos
region.zh: 韋旺里烏與冥府（珀勒圖伊），布吉宇宙

texts.period: La Galigo epic tradition (Bugis); c. 14th century origins

source.archive: UNESCO Memory of the World Register (La Galigo)
source.work: La Galigo epic; the death of Sawerigading

summary.en: The Sawerigading cycle ends downward: the hero's returning ship breaks, and he does not drown but descends — taken to the underworld, where he becomes its king. The greatest hero of the middle world thus ends as the ruler of the level beneath it, closing the La Galigo's geography of three worlds with a king in each.
summary.zh: 薩維里加丁故事以向下收束：歸舟破碎，英雄未被溺斃而是下行——被接入冥府，並成為冥府之王。中界之至高英雄終為下界之君，使《加利戈》三界之地理各得一王而閉合。

passages.text: The ship of Sawerigading's return breaks, and the hero is not lost but taken: he descends to the underworld of the Bugis cosmos, where he becomes its king. The middle world's greatest hero thus ends as ruler of the level beneath it — the epic's three worlds each with its sovereign, and death transposed from drowning into coronation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the La Galigo Sawerigading cycle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The journey of the hero Sawerigading and his son La Galigo to Senrijawa is the complete episode of the La Galigo preserved in the manuscript of the Museum La Galigo at Makassar — a voyage through the epic's sea of courts, storms and ceremonies. Father and son travel the water-world of the Bugis epic, meeting the powers and courts that mark its geography; the episode carries the work's pattern of voyage, obligation and return that governs the whole La Galigo.

title.en: Toar and Lumimu'ut: The Mother and Son Who Peopled Minahassa
title.zh: 托阿爾與盧米穆特：繁衍米納哈薩的母子

region.zh: 北蘇拉威西米納哈薩半島

texts.period: Minahassa ancestral tradition; recorded in nineteenth-twentieth century ethnography

source.archive: Minahassa oral tradition (recorded in colonial-era ethnography)
source.work: The ancestral myth of Toar and Lumimu'ut (Minahassa tradition)

summary.en: The Minahassa begin with a mother and a son: Lumimu'ut, the first woman of the land, and her son Toar, who grew to be a giant. Separated so that neither knew the other's origin, mother and son met as strangers on the mountain, wed, and their children became the first peoples of the peninsula — the sibling-creator pair of North Sulawesi, whose boundary-taboo is told before every genealogy.
summary.zh: 米納哈薩以一對母子開篇：大地初女盧米穆特與其子托阿爾——長成巨人。母子相隔、互不知來歷，竟在山上如陌生人相遇而結合；其子孫遂為半島最早的族群——北蘇拉威西之『兄妹創世對』，其禁忌故事在每一份譜系之前被講述。

sensitivity.note: Minahassa ancestry charter; the incest-recognition pair is treated at tradition level.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the standard Minahassa ancestral account; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Minahassa peoples of the northern peninsula tell their beginnings as a story of two people who did not know what they were to each other.

BEGINNING: THE FIRST WOMAN AND HER SON. Lumimu'ut is the first woman of the Minahassa country; her son Toar grows in the wilds to marvellous size and strength. The two live apart, and the tale keeps them apart by a device: neither is ever told the origin of the other — the son does not know his mother, the mother does not know her grown son.

MIDDLE: THE MEETING ON THE MOUNTAIN. Mother and son meet as strangers on the mountain, exchange the courtesies of two young unmarried people, and wed. Only afterwards, when the signs of kinship are told to them by the old ones — in the standard tellings, by the story of the twin stones or the staffs of Lumimu'ut — do they understand what they have done.

END: THE CHILDREN AND THE DIVISION. The children of the union are the first peoples of the peninsula; their mother, understanding now the true relation of all the houses, gathers her descendants and divides them — the division told of in the companion record of the stone of Watu Pinawetengan — and the Minahassa nations set out from the mountain each to their own lands.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) provides the sibling-creator pair of North Sulawesi; (2) uses the not-knowing device to keep the ancestral union within the law; (3) grounds the Minahassa nations' division of the land in the mother's act of ordering; and (4) makes genealogy-telling itself the ritual that repairs the broken knowledge. The Minahassa tellings keep the recognition mechanism visible rather than mysterious: in the standard forms, the tokens that reveal the kinship are Lumimu'ut's own — the twin staffs or stones by which a mother may know her son, held apart by the same device that kept the origin untold. The not-knowing is thus presented as an institution with a purpose: the first union is lawful because the law was not yet knowable, and the knowledge that arrives afterward is converted into the division of the children, the mother ordering her descendants to their lands. The stone of Watu Pinawetengan, with its old inscriptions, is the charter's monument: the place of division where Tonsea, Tondano, Tombulu and Tontemboan received their allotments. In Minahassa memory the myth does its work at every genealogy-recitation, where telling the descent is itself the rite that repairs the first broken knowledge — the community listening to the origin it once could not be told.
narrative.zh: 北蘇拉威西半島米納哈薩人以其開端為一對互不知身份者之故事。開篇：初女盧米穆特與其子在荒野中生長，成為力大無窮之巨人；二者分居，且故事以一設計使之相隔：誰也不被告知對方之來歷。中段：母子如陌生人於山上相遇，行未婚青年之禮而結合；及長者（標準敘述中為孿生石或盧米穆特之杖的故事）點明親緣之徵，二人方知所為。結尾：結合之子孫即半島最早之族群；母親既明諸家真實關係，乃聚其後裔而分之（其分地之事見『瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石』篇）；米納哈薩各族遂自聖山而出，各赴其土。功能：供給北蘇拉威西之兄妹創世對、以『不知情』維繫祖源結合之合法性、以母親之秩序行為奠立米納哈薩民族分地之憲章、並使譜系講述本身成為修復所斷知識之儀式。

Makes genealogy-telling the ritual that repairs the broken knowledge

title.en: The Stone of Watu Pinawetengan: Where the Peoples Were Divided
title.zh: 瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石：分族之地

region.en: Watu Pinawetengan stone, Tomohon, North Sulawesi
region.zh: 北蘇拉威西托莫洪瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石

source.work: The tradition of Watu Pinawetengan (Minahassa stone of division)

summary.en: On the stone called Watu Pinawetengan — 'the place of division' — the first ancestress or the first ancestors gathered the descendants and marked out their lands: the four directions of the Minahassa peoples, the allotment of Tonsea, Tondano, Tombulu and Tontemboan. The stone still stands, its old inscriptions the charter of the peninsula's ethnography.
summary.zh: 在名為『分族之地』的瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石上，初祖召集後裔、劃定各土：米納哈薩四向之民——通塞亞、通達諾、通布盧與通特姆布安之分配。石仍矗立，其古刻即半島族群地圖之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Living sacred site of the Minahassa; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: On the stone of Watu Pinawetengan the first ancestress gathered her descendants and divided the lands among them, fixing the allotments of the Minahassa peoples to the four directions. The stone still stands with its old inscriptions, and the Minahassa nations tell their origins from that place of division — genealogy, land and monument joined in one charter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minahassa tradition of Watu Pinawetengan; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Minahassa tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tumanurung of Gowa: The One Who Descended
title.zh: 戈瓦之圖瑪努倫：降臨者

region.zh: 南蘇拉威西戈瓦（望加錫）

texts.period: Makassar lontara' chronicle tradition (Gowa dynastic origins)

source.work: The Tumanurung narrative of the Gowa chronicle (Makassar dynastic tradition)

summary.en: The founding myth of the Makassar kingdom of Gowa: a woman of heavenly radiance, the Tumanurung ('the one who descended'), appears in the land and is found by the people; she is wed to the chief and bears the line of the kings of Gowa — the white-blooded ancestress whose descent from above legitimizes the Makassar throne.
summary.zh: 望加錫戈瓦王國之開基神話：一位天光燦然之女子——『圖瑪努倫』（降臨者）——現於此地為民所見；她與酋長成婚，誕下戈瓦歷代國王之世系——這位血統純白、自天而降的女祖，為望加錫王座賦予合法性。

sensitivity.note: Dynastic charter of the Gowa chronicle tradition.

passages.text: The people of the land find a woman of heavenly radiance, the Tumanurung, 'the one who descended,' and cannot tell where she has come from; the chief takes her to wife, and from the marriage descends the line of the kings of Gowa. The descended ancestress is the charter of the Makassar throne: her children carry the whiteness and radiance of her origin, and the kingdom's legitimacy is told as descent rather than conquest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gowa chronicle's Tumanurung narrative; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Gowa chronicle tradition; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tongkonan and the Horns: Toraja Houses That Remember
title.zh: 通科南與牛角：會記憶的托拉查之屋

region.zh: 南蘇拉威西塔納托拉查高地

texts.period: Toraja aluk to dolo tradition; recorded in twentieth-century ethnography

source.work: The tradition of the tongkonan ancestral house and the buffalo-horn genealogy (Toraja)

summary.en: The great boat-shaped houses of the Toraja (tongkonan) are not dwellings but genealogies: each is founded by an ancestor, oriented to the points of the Toraja cosmos, and its facade grows outward in horns — every pair of buffalo horns sacrificed at the house's feasts and funerals a further record of who owed and gave what to the family. The house remembers so that the living need not: rank, debt and descent are read off the wall.
summary.zh: 托拉查人船形大屋（tongkonan）非宅第而是譜系：每座由一位祖先奠基，朝向托拉查宇宙之方位；其立面以牛角向外生長——屋中歷次慶典與葬禮所宰水牛之每一對角，皆為『誰欠何物、誰予何物』之紀錄。屋替活人記憶：階級、債務與世系皆可自牆上讀出。

sensitivity.note: Living Toraja material religion; paraphrase respectfully, note the funeral economy without exoticizing it.

passages.text: The tongkonan houses of the Toraja are founded by named ancestors and oriented to the cosmos; the house is the family's seat of memory, not merely its shelter. At every great feast and funeral, buffalo are sacrificed and their horns added to the facade; the growing wall of horns is a public genealogy of the house — rank, debt and descent read off the architecture itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Toraja tongkonan tradition as recorded in twentieth-century ethnography; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Toraja tongkonan tradition; not verbatim.
